points.t: Fixed ‘target’ lesions with three zones on the palms, backs of hands, forearms or feet, often 1–3 weeks after a cold sore.
Cell-mediated reaction to HSV antigen in the skin (most cases); *Mycoplasma* in children; drugs are uncommon.
Supportive care, potent topical steroid, mouthwashes and analgesia; aciclovir for active HSV; suppressive antiviral for recurrent HSV-EM.
SJS/TEN: atypical flat dusky targets, widespread skin pain, blistering and mucosal erosions after a new drug.

points: Predominantly a **type IV (cell-mediated / delayed)** hypersensitivity reaction.
**HSV-1/2** is the leading association (often 1–3 weeks after herpes labialis/genitalis; recurrent EM with recurrent HSV).
Other infections: *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* (esp. children/young adults with respiratory prodrome), less often other viruses/bacteria.
Drugs can rarely trigger EM-like eruptions, but severe drug blistering disease should be managed as SJS/TEN pathway until proven otherwise.
Circulating immune response to microbial antigen → cytotoxic T-cell attack on keratinocytes → epidermal necrosis in the target centre.
**Typical target:** ≤ 3 cm, round, **three zones** — dark-red/dusky (sometimes blistered or crusted) centre → paler oedematous ring → outer red ring with a sharp edge.
**Raised atypical target:** two zones, palpable — still EM.
**Flat atypical targets / purpuric macules, widespread on trunk** → think **SJS/TEN** (drug-related), especially with mucosal erosions or skin pain.
Palms: thick stratum corneum can make targets look flatter and more "bruise-like"; the iris pattern is often easiest to see here.
**Diagnosis:** erythema multiforme **minor** (typical acral targets, polymorphous papules, **no mucosal involvement**).

History: recent HSV, *Mycoplasma*/respiratory symptoms, drugs, mucosal symptoms, eye symptoms.
Exam: full skin + oral + eyes + genitals.
Investigate if atypical / severe: *Mycoplasma* testing if respiratory; HSV swabs of cold sores; consider biopsy if uncertain.

cards.name: Urticaria / urticaria multiforme
cards.clue: Migratory weals <24 h; no fixed dusky necrotic centre

cards.name: SJS / TEN
cards.clue: Flat atypical targets, widespread purpuric macules, sheet-like denudation; usually **drugs**; severe systemic illness

cards.name: Fixed drug eruption
cards.clue: Round dusky plaque(s) at same site on re-challenge

cards.name: Secondary syphilis / other
cards.clue: Check risk history; serology if unsure

points: Emollients; bland oral care (soft diet, antiseptic/analgesic mouth rinses per local advice) for oral EM.
Analgesia; rest; treat concurrent HSV cold sore if active (topical/oral antivirals per licence/BNF).
Document drug history; stop any newly started suspect drug pending specialist advice if morphology atypical.
Mild cutaneous EM: often supportive only in primary care.
Recurrent HSV-associated EM: dermatology may consider continuous or intermittent **oral antiviral prophylaxis** (e.g. aciclovir — specialist/experienced initiation).
**Urgent same-day / emergency** if: extensive mucosal disease impairing intake, ocular involvement, suspected SJS/TEN, systemic toxicity, inability to distinguish from severe drug reaction.
Ophthalmology review for eye involvement.
IP: do **not** start systemic steroids for presumed EM without specialist advice (may be used in selected severe cases under derm).

items.t: Mucosal erosions (mouth, eyes, genitals) with skin pain, blistering or skin loss: possible **SJS/TEN**, so stop suspect drugs and admit the same day.
Unable to eat or drink: admission for fluids and analgesia.

pearls.t: Teach patients with recurrent cold sores that EM can follow HSV — early antiviral for prodromal HSV may reduce triggers (individualise).
Emphasise difference between EM major and SJS — reduces panic but does not delay referral when severe.
Warn that scars are uncommon but pigment change can linger.
Pregnancy: check BNF for any antivirals/steroids contemplated.
